title: England Have Never Won a T20 World Cup at Home. Australia Have Never Lost a Final. Something Breaks at Lord's on Sunday.
excerpt: The Women's T20 World Cup final between hosts England and six-time champions Australia at Lord's is the biggest match in the tournament's history — and Indian fans have their own reasons to keep watching.
body:
Lord's on a Sunday in July, with a World Cup on the line. It doesn't get bigger than this.

England will face Australia in the final of the ICC Women's T20 World Cup on Sunday, July 5, at the Home of Cricket — a venue that has never before hosted a women's T20 international of this magnitude. It is, by every measure, the most significant match in the history of this tournament.

England are in a Women's T20 World Cup final for the first time since 2018, when they lost to Australia in Antigua. Australia, for their part, are seeking a seventh title. They have appeared in seven finals and won six. Their only loss came in the very first edition, in 2009 — to England. The symmetry is almost too neat.

## Sciver-Brunt's Tournament

If England are to win, they will likely need Nat Sciver-Brunt to do what she has done all tournament: carry the batting when others falter. In Thursday's semifinal against South Africa at The Oval, she walked in at 23-3, her calf strapped and her World Cup participation in doubt until 48 hours earlier. She walked out with 75 off 47 balls and a Player of the Match award, having shared a 133-run stand with Heather Knight that turned the innings on its head.

Sciver-Brunt has been England's most important batter for three years now. But this tournament, on home soil, feels like her coronation. If she delivers one more performance like Thursday's, the narrative writes itself.

> **"Five days after the final, Lord's will host a historic women's Test between England and India starting July 10 — the first time a women's Test has ever been played at cricket's most iconic venue."**

## Australia's Machine

Australia do not do drama. They do efficiency. In their semifinal, Ash Gardner and Ellyse Perry dismantled West Indies with the kind of clinical precision that has defined their dominance of the women's game for a decade. Sophie Molineux's captaincy has been unflashy but effective — rotate the bowlers, build pressure, and trust that the batting depth will always be enough.

They have won their last 14 T20 World Cup matches stretching back to 2022. The streak includes demolitions of India, South Africa, and New Zealand. No team has found a consistent blueprint to beat them in knockout cricket.

![Home of Cricket — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/77/Lords-Cricket-Ground-Pavilion-06-08-2017.jpg)

That is the challenge England face on Sunday: not just a team, but a culture of winning that has no parallel in women's cricket.

## India's Stake in This Final

India's tournament ended in the group stage — a result that has already triggered calls for change, with former selector Diana Edulji publicly demanding the sacking of captain Harmanpreet Kaur and coach Amol Muzumdar. But the Indian connection to this final runs deeper than the scoreboard.

Five days after the final, Lord's will host a historic women's Test between England and India starting July 10 — the first time a women's Test has ever been played at cricket's most iconic venue. For the tens of thousands of Indian-origin fans across Britain, the back-to-back events at Lord's offer a rare week of women's cricket at the sport's spiritual home.

The tournament has already shattered records. More than 160,000 tickets have been sold across the event — more than double the attendance of the 2017 Women's World Cup in England. A crowd of 27,000 packed Lord's for the final group-stage double-header. The MCC's chief executive Robert Lawson has written personally to members urging them to fill the Pavilion on Sunday, anxious to avoid a repeat of the embarrassingly sparse members' section during the 2017 final — the one India lost to England by nine runs.

## The Stage

Rita Ora will headline the closing ceremony from 2:30 PM local time, with Clean Bandit performing after the match. The final begins at 3 PM BST — that's 7:30 PM IST and 10 AM ET.

For diaspora cricket fans in the UK, this is the weekend to be at Lord's. For those watching from the US, it's a Sunday morning appointment with history.

Australia are the favourites. They almost always are. But Lord's has a way of bending narratives. And England, at home, with Sciver-Brunt at the crease — they believe they can break the pattern.
